title: Listening practice: An experiment, a debate and a poem form
description: Three recordings: a lab group presents evidence for a claim, a class debates a history question, and a student presents a poem form.

stimuli.title: Listen: A group shares its experiment

turns.speaker: Jun
turns.text: Our claim is that the foam cup keeps water warm the best. We filled each cup with water at seventy degrees Celsius and measured again after twenty minutes.

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: The foam cup dropped from seventy to fifty-eight degrees, so it lost twelve degrees. The paper cup lost nineteen, and the metal cup lost twenty-eight.

turns.speaker: Ms. Banerjee
turns.text: Those are clear numbers. But can you be sure the cups, and not something else, caused the difference?

turns.speaker: Jun
turns.text: Good question. We used the same amount of water in every cup, and we kept all three on the same table, away from the window. So the material was the only thing that changed.

turns.speaker: Sofia
turns.text: Also, we repeated the test twice, and the order of the results stayed the same. That makes our claim stronger.

turns.speaker: Ms. Banerjee
turns.text: I agree. One more suggestion: next time, test a glass cup too.

stimuli.title: Listen: A class debate

turns.speaker: Mr. Hall
turns.text: Today's debate question is: were Roman roads the most important reason the Roman Empire stayed united? Nadia, please go first.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: I say yes. Roman roads let soldiers march quickly to trouble spots, so rebellions could be stopped early. In addition, messengers could carry orders across the empire much faster than before. Without the roads, the emperor would have lost control of faraway provinces.

turns.speaker: Omar
turns.text: I respectfully disagree. Roads mattered, but a shared legal system and a common currency mattered more. People in many provinces followed Roman law, and they could pay with the same coins. Roads can't hold an empire together if people don't trust the rules.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's a fair point, but laws and coins also needed the roads to travel across the empire.

turns.speaker: Mr. Hall
turns.text: Thank you both. Let's hear from the audience.

Without the roads, the emperor would have lost control of faraway provinces. Omar: I respectfully disagree. Roads mattered, but a shared legal system and a common currency mattered more. People in many provinces followed Roman law, and they could pay with the same coins. Roads can't hold an empire together if people don't trust the rules. Nadia: That's a fair point, but laws and coins also needed the roads to travel across the empire. Mr. Hall: Thank you both. Let's hear from the audience.

stimuli.title: Listen: A presentation about a kind of poem

turns.speaker: Hana
turns.text: For my presentation, I'm going to describe a poem form called haiku. Haiku began in Japan hundreds of years ago. Traditionally, a haiku has three short lines. In English, writers often follow a pattern of five syllables in the first line, seven in the second, and five in the third. Many haiku are about nature, and many mention a season, like the first snow or summer rain. What makes haiku special is that it captures just one moment, so the poet doesn't explain feelings. Instead, the poet shows an image and lets the reader feel something. For example, a haiku might describe a single leaf floating down a stream, and the reader imagines the rest. Next week, you'll write your own, so remember: three lines, an image from nature, and one moment.

items.stem: How long did the group wait before measuring the water again?

options.text: Ten minutes
Twenty minutes
Thirty minutes
Forty minutes

distractors.a: Jun says the group measured again after twenty minutes, not ten.
distractors.c: Jun says the group measured again after twenty minutes, not thirty.
distractors.d: Jun says the group measured again after twenty minutes, not forty.

items.explanation: Jun says the group filled each cup with water at seventy degrees Celsius and measured again after twenty minutes.

support.clue: Listen to Jun's first two sentences. Jun says the claim, and then tells when the group measured again.
support.frame: The group measured the water again after ______ minutes.
support.model: Mentor example. 'We watered the bean plant and measured it again after three days.' A speaker can say how much time passed between two measurements. Listen for the time between the group's measurements.

facts: The cup experiment and its results are invented for this practice item.

misconceptions.a: gives a number that was not said
misconceptions.c: gives a number that was not said
misconceptions.d: gives a number that was not said

items.stem: Match each cup to the evidence the group gives.
items.explanation: Sofia says the foam cup lost twelve degrees, the paper cup lost nineteen, and the metal cup lost twenty-eight.

support.clue: Listen to Sofia's first turn. She says three numbers, one for each cup.
support.model: Mentor example. A table shows Plant A grew 4 centimeters and Plant B grew 7 centimeters. You can say, "Plant A grew 4 centimeters." Match each cup to its number the same way.

facts: 70 - 58 = 12, 70 - 51 = 19, and 70 - 42 = 28 degrees Celsius of heat lost.
The cup experiment and its results are invented for this practice item.

items.stem: Why does Jun say they used the same amount of water and the same table?

options.text: To make the cup material the only thing that changed.
To show the water started at seventy degrees Celsius.
To show that the test was repeated twice.
To show that all three cups are the same.

distractors.b: The starting temperature is a different detail; this point is about making the test fair.
distractors.c: Sofia, not Jun, mentions the repeat, and it is a different point.
distractors.d: The cups are different materials; that is what the group is testing.

items.explanation: Jun keeps the water amount and table location the same, so the material is the only thing that changed and must have caused the difference.

support.clue: Listen to Jun's answer after the teacher asks whether the cups caused the difference.
support.frame: Jun keeps the water and the table the same because ______.
support.model: Mentor example. 'We practiced with the same ball every day so we could compare our scores fairly.' A speaker explains why one part is kept the same. Explain Jun's reason in the same way.

facts: A fair test changes only one variable and keeps the others the same.

misconceptions.d: misses the purpose of the test

options.text: Laws mattered more than roads.
The empire did not stay together.
Common coins held the empire together.
Roads held the empire together.

distractors.a: That is Omar's view, not Nadia's.
distractors.b: Both students agree the empire stayed united; they disagree about the reason.
distractors.c: Omar gives this reason; Nadia says coins also needed roads.

items.explanation: Nadia says yes to the debate question: roads were the most important reason the empire stayed united.

support.clue: Listen to Nadia's first words, 'I say yes.' Then listen to the reasons she gives.
support.frame: Nadia agrees with the debate question. She says that ______ ______.
support.model: Mentor example. "I believe good lighting is the main reason the theater feels safe at night." A speaker gives an opinion first and a reason after. Find Nadia's opinion.

facts: The Roman Empire built a large network of roads that soldiers and messengers used.
Roman coins were used across the empire.

items.stem: Sort each reason: is it Nadia's or Omar's?

tokens.text: Soldiers could march quickly to trouble spots.
People in many provinces followed Roman law.
Messengers carried orders across the empire.
People could pay with the same coins.

items.explanation: Nadia talks about soldiers and messengers on the roads. Omar talks about shared laws and shared coins.

support.clue: Nadia speaks first, after I say yes. Omar speaks after I respectfully disagree. Sort what each person says.
support.frame: Nadia's reasons are about ______. Omar's reasons are about ______.
support.model: Mentor example. In a debate about school uniforms, one student says "it saves families money" and another says "it limits how students express themselves." Listen to who says what, and sort each reason by speaker.

facts: Roman roads let armies and messengers travel quickly.
Roman law and a common currency applied across many provinces of the empire, although local laws and customs also continued.

items.stem: How does Nadia answer Omar's argument?

options.text: She agrees that laws mattered more than roads.
She says laws and coins also needed a way to travel.
She says the laws were written before the coins.
She asks the audience to end the debate.

distractors.a: She says fair point but keeps her own position.
distractors.c: She makes no claim about which was created first.
distractors.d: Mr. Hall, not Nadia, invites the audience to speak.

items.explanation: Nadia says Omar's point is fair, but she argues that laws and coins also needed the roads to travel across the empire.

support.clue: Listen to Nadia's last turn. The words fair point, but show she accepts one part and then disagrees.
support.frame: Nadia accepts one part of Omar's point, but she adds that ______.
support.model: Mentor example. "That's a good point about cost, but a longer lunch would also help students eat slowly." A speaker can accept a point and then add a new one. Listen for what Nadia adds.

misconceptions.a: reads a partial agreement as full agreement
misconceptions.c: adds a claim that was not made

items.stem: According to Hana, how does the poet make the reader feel something?

options.text: Tells a long story with a surprise ending
Uses rhyme at the end of each line
Shows an image for the reader to feel
Describes the poet's own life

distractors.a: Hana says a haiku captures just one moment. It is not a long story.
distractors.d: Hana says the poet shows an image from the moment, not the poet's own life.

items.explanation: Hana says the poet does not explain feelings. Instead, the poet shows an image and lets the reader feel something.

support.clue: Listen near the end of Hana's description, right after the word Instead.
support.frame: The poet ______ and lets the reader ______.
support.model: Mentor example. 'A good photograph does not say, This is a happy day. It shows children laughing.' A speaker can say what a creator shows instead of what the creator explains. Listen for what the poet does in a haiku.

facts: Haiku is a Japanese poem form with three short lines.
A haiku captures a single moment through an image.

misconceptions.a: adds a feature that was not said
misconceptions.b: adds a feature that was not said
misconceptions.d: adds a feature that was not said

items.stem: Which two things does Hana say are true of many haiku?

options.text: They capture one moment.
They explain the poet's feelings.
They always rhyme.
Many of them mention a season.

distractors.b: Hana says the poet shows an image instead of explaining feelings.

items.explanation: Hana says many haiku mention a season and that a haiku captures just one moment.

support.clue: Listen to the sentence about seasons and to what Hana says makes haiku special. One choice says the opposite of what she says.
support.frame: Hana says haiku show ______ and many mention ______.
support.model: Mentor example. "A recipe lists the ingredients and gives the steps in order." A speaker can list features of a type of text. Listen for two features Hana lists and choose the matching sentences.

facts: Many haiku are about nature and mention a season.
A haiku captures a single moment through an image.

misconceptions.c: adds a feature that was not mentioned
